translationRepairs: When the Marquis of Jiang left court, he hastened from the hall with an air of immense self-satisfaction.
When the Marquis of Jiang, who was chancellor, left court, he hastened from the hall with an air of immense self-satisfaction.
絳侯為丞相 explicitly makes him chancellor; the omission leaves the next question about the chancellor without antecedent.
The emperor also rose and rose again.
The emperor was also angry and rose.
Received editions read 上亦怒，起, not dittographic 上亦起，起; collapsing to a single 'rose' still omits 怒.
After the defeat of Wu and Chu, the throne named a younger son of Prince Yuan—Marquis Pinglu—as king of Chu and gave Yuan Ang the chancellorship of that kingdom.
After Wu and Chu were defeated, the emperor made Prince Yuan’s son, Marquis Pinglu Li, King of Chu and appointed Yuan Ang chancellor of Chu.
元王子平陸侯禮 names Li as a son of Prince Yuan and Marquis of Pinglu. The old version invents birth order and omits his given name.

Emperor Wen commended him and bestowed on Cuo an imperial edict written on jade with a gracious reply, saying, "The emperor inquires of the household commandant of the heir apparent: your memorial setting forth the three divisions of military principle has been received.

Emperor Wen commended him and bestowed on Cuo a sealed imperial edict with a gracious reply, saying, "The emperor inquires of the household commandant of the heir apparent: your memorial setting forth the three divisions of military principle has been received.
璽書 is a sealed imperial edict; 'written on jade' misreads 璽 as a jade writing surface.

The board of recommenders—Marquis of Pingyang Cao Kui, Marquis of Ruoyin, Marquis of Yingyin Guan He, the minister of justice Yichang, the governor of Longxi Kunxie—placed your servant Chao Cuo on the list. I kowtow twice and say: every sage king sought helpers; the Yellow Emperor won Limu and led the Five Thearchs, Yu won Gao Yao and founded the Three Dynasties, Huan won Guan Zhong and headed the Five Hegemons.

The men who recommended me as Worthy and Good were your servants the Marquis of Pingyang, Cao Zhu; the Marquis of Ruyin, Xiahou Zao; the Marquis of Yingyin, Guan He; the Commandant of Justice, Yichang; and the Administrator of Longxi, Kunxie. Your servant Chao Cuo bows twice and, risking death, states: I have heard that every worthy ruler of antiquity sought worthy men as his wings and helpers. Thus the Yellow Emperor obtained Limu and became foremost of the Five Thearchs; Great Yu obtained Gao Yao and became progenitor of the Three Kings; and Duke Huan of Qi obtained Guan Zhong and became leader of the Five Hegemons.
The marquises are Cao Zhu (曹窋) and Xiahou Zao (夏侯灶), not Cao Kui and the invented Shen Zao. The revision also preserves the memorial's syntax and corrects 三王祖.
the First Emperor preened while ministers cringed, pride swelled, peril went unseen;
its ruler vaunted his own worth while his ministers, afraid, flattered him; swollen with arrogance, he gave himself free rein and ignored impending disaster;
The passage concerns Qin but makes its ruler the acting subject. 'The First Emperor' is too specific, while treating the polity itself as vain and flattered produces awkward English.
When the age turned and counsel over Wu and Chu came into play, he leaned too hard on sharp speech and paid with his life.
By then times had changed. In the matter of Wu, he relied too boldly on argument, and his own career ended in failure.
及吳壹說 refers to the matter of Wu, not Wu and Chu. 身亦不遂 says his own career did not prosper; 'paid with his life' is stronger than the source.
